worst_places.after: httpOnly solves exactly one problem: JS can't read the cookie. It also creates exactly one new one. **The browser sends that cookie automatically on every request to the domain, no matter who started the request.** That includes a request started by a malicious page the user opened in another tab — the attack known as CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). The general CSRF mechanism is covered in the [Security] topic; here we only look at what it means for an auth cookie.

worst_places.quote: Key decisions: (1) Multi-tenancy — if you expect a small number of large enterprise customers with individual requirements (their own Identity Provider, custom login branding, strict compliance) — realm-per-tenant, despite the growing operational load; if it's a self-serve model with many small tenants — a shared realm with group-based isolation and a `tenant_id` claim that's mandatorily filtered on EVERY Resource Server request.
worst_places.problem: The whole answer is one 178-word paragraph holding five numbered decisions, each a multi-clause sentence with its own parenthetical and em-dashed condition. Rendered on a phone it is a solid block of grey with no visual anchor for «(1)…(5)», so a reader who pauses mid-answer cannot find their place. The parallel ru answer has the same shape. This is the pattern behind the 25 over-long paragraphs and 2 theory walls the script flags in file 11.
worst_places.before: Key decisions: (1) Multi-tenancy — if you expect a small number of large enterprise customers with individual requirements (their own Identity Provider, custom login branding, strict compliance) — realm-per-tenant, despite the growing operational load; if it's a self-serve model with many small tenants — a shared realm with group-based isolation and a `tenant_id` claim that's mandatorily filtered on EVERY Resource Server request. (2) Token storage — given real security requirements (typical for B2B SaaS with corporate customers), start directly with the BFF pattern rather than a public client in the browser — it removes a whole class of problems (XSS token theft, silent-check-sso's third-party cookie fragility) architecturally.
worst_places.after:
Five decisions:

**1. Multi-tenancy.** A few large enterprise customers → realm-per-tenant. Each of them needs its own Identity Provider, its own login branding, and its own compliance story, and that's worth the growing operational load. A self-serve model with many small tenants → one shared realm, isolation by group, and a `tenant_id` claim in the token. In that case the Resource Server must filter by `tenant_id` on every single request.

**2. Token storage.** Start with the BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) pattern, not a public client in the browser. B2B SaaS with corporate customers has real security requirements, and the BFF removes a whole class of problems architecturally: an XSS attack has no token to steal, and silent-check-sso's third-party cookie fragility never arises.

worst_places.quote: **PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced "pixy," RFC 7636) was originally designed for mobile apps, but today Keycloak and most modern guidance recommend it for ALL clients, confidential ones included — because it defends against a specific class of attack (authorization code interception) that's relevant regardless of client type, not "the absence of a secret."
worst_places.problem: 85 words before the first full stop, at the exact moment the reader meets the acronym for the first time: an expansion, a pronunciation note, an RFC number, a history claim, a current-practice claim, a mechanism claim, and a rebuttal of a wrong belief — all in one breath. The rebuttal («not "the absence of a secret"») lands 70 words after the thing it rebuts, so its referent is lost.
worst_places.before: **PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced "pixy," RFC 7636) was originally designed for mobile apps, but today Keycloak and most modern guidance recommend it for ALL clients, confidential ones included — because it defends against a specific class of attack (authorization code interception) that's relevant regardless of client type, not "the absence of a secret."
worst_places.after: **PKCE** stands for Proof Key for Code Exchange (pronounced "pixy", RFC 7636). It was originally designed for mobile apps. Today Keycloak and most modern guidance recommend it for every client, confidential ones included. The reason isn't "a public client has no secret". PKCE defends against a specific class of attack — authorization code interception — and that attack is possible whatever the client type.

patterns: ALL-CAPS is the zone's default emphasis device, and it is used 228 times in prose alone across the 22 files (plus more inside the ASCII diagram blocks): EN shouts WANTS / GOT / WHAT / WHO / EVERY / SAME / ENTIRE / MUST / ON TOP / SIMULTANEOUSLY, RU shouts ХОЧЕТ / КАЖДЫЙ / НИКОГДА / АБСОЛЮТНО / ВООБЩЕ / ОДНОЙ / МЕХАНИЗМ. Because everything is emphasized, nothing is — and on a phone it reads as an angry voice. It also corrupts the tooling: a large share of the script's 344 'unexpanded abbreviations' for this zone are these caps words (EVERY, GOT, WHO, TOP, WANTS, BEFORE, OLD, WHICH…), not acronyms. Fix: **bold** for the load-bearing word, caps only for real acronyms and literal config values (SAMEORIGIN, S256).

The zone's default sentence shape is 'lead clause — em-dash — second independent clause — parenthetical containing a cross-reference to another article — em-dash — consequence', carrying three or four facts. This is why EN runs 43-60% of sentences over 25 words (file 06 at 60%, with a 98-word sentence) and RU 28-45% over 28 words. The parenthetical cross-references are the main accelerant: nearly every explanatory paragraph carries one or two '(see article 0X)' / '(статья 0X)' asides, which both lengthen the sentence and interrupt exactly the reader the site targets — someone reading in short bursts. Fix: one fact per sentence; move the cross-reference to its own short sentence at the end of the paragraph.

Almost every acronym is spelled out exactly once, in the article that introduces the concept, and then used bare in the other ten files. PKCE is expanded in 01 and used 9× bare in 07; JWKS is expanded in 03 and used 5× bare in 04; XSS is used 8× in 06 (the article whose whole argument rests on it) and never expanded; TTL appears 5× in 03 and 4× in 11 unexpanded. Since files are read out of order, the first use in each file needs a three-word gloss. The cheatsheet (10) and the question bank (11) are worst hit — 20 and 30 bare acronyms respectively.

The ru locale carries machine-translation residue that a reader will notice: six English words spliced into Russian sentences ('over логированием' 04:20, 'either … либо' 03:318, 'even если' 05:102, 'requires БД lookup' 03:133, 'не safer по умолчанию' 06:76, 'architectural дефект' 06:179), four mixed-alphabet typos ('raньше' 01:300, 'upскорить' 03:141, 'статeless' 04:329, 'Chuжой' 07:62), and one mistranslated core term ('Резервный сервер' for Resource Server, 01:130). A single grep pass over the ru files for Latin-script function words and for words mixing Cyrillic with Latin letters would catch all eleven.

Every one of the nine conceptual articles opens with a meta section ('Зачем без этого нельзя…' / 'Why you can't write secure auth code without this', 'Зачем разбираться в модели, а не сразу лезть в код') that spends two or three paragraphs justifying the article before stating a single fact. Section-level leads inside the articles are good (definition first, caveats after) — it is specifically the article opener that makes the reader scroll past positioning to reach content. Fix: one sentence of 'what this article answers', then the first real claim.
notes: Depth and structure are the zone's strength and should not be touched: diagram/code rhythm is genuinely good (theory_walls=0 in articles 01-10), and the trade-off framing (honest 'X isn't free' sections) is exactly right for the target reader. Two non-language defects worth a ticket anyway: the code snippets for UmaPermissionGuard (04) and StepUpGuard (08) use this.reflector without injecting it, in both locales, so they don't compile; and file 10's grant-type table has five cells in a four-column row while its Part 2 comparison rows run to 661 characters (ru) / 423 (en). ASCII diagrams run 79-137 characters wide (01's discovery JSON is 137) and the outer boxes in 01 and 02 have misaligned right borders — both hurt the phone reader the rubric describes.
